strengths: The task is practically relevant: generating stylized Gaussian scenes from unposed images without per-scene optimization would simplify 3D content creation.
Separating frozen geometry prediction from style-conditioned appearance is a sensible design. Qualitative examples demonstrate varied artistic effects while retaining recognizable scene structure.
Table 3 reports consistently better short- and long-range consistency than the evaluated baselines, and ArtScore improves on three of four scenes.
The paper includes component ablations, held-out category and scene evaluations, extensive visual examples, and inference-time and memory measurements.
weaknesses: The central attention distinction is mathematically unsupported as written. In Eqs. 1–2, standard cross-attention with identical style keys and values operates independently on each query, so concatenating queries across views produces the same outputs as processing each view separately. An additional operation or architectural difference is needed to explain the claimed cross-view coupling and Table 1 results.

The proposed 3D loss has a substantial specification inconsistency. Equation 6 describes statistics after multi-view voxel fusion, but Algorithm 3 voxelizes each view separately and sums its statistics-matching loss. The pseudocode therefore does not implement the claimed cross-view fusion. Moreover, matching global moments of fused features does not itself enforce agreement between corresponding views.

The evaluation does not adequately establish the claimed balance of style fidelity, content preservation, and consistency. ArtScore measures reference-free artness rather than similarity to the requested style. The LPIPS/RMSE protocol omits explicit correspondence, warping, and occlusion handling; without these details, improvements are difficult to interpret and could reflect smoother outputs.

Comparisons cover only two scene-specific baselines and four scenes, with one baseline missing a scene. The unavailable concurrent Styl3R implementation reasonably explains its omission, but the paper still lacks a controlled baseline using the same reconstruction backbone with a simpler appearance-conditioning method to isolate its contribution.

Ablations provide limited support for the central claims. Attention variants are evaluated through style-free RGB reconstruction rather than stylization, and RGB metrics do not directly establish better geometry. The voxel-loss gains are modest, without variability estimates, and contributions from CLIP supervision and the two-stage training strategy are not isolated.

Reproducibility is insufficient despite the supplied pseudocode: optimizer settings, training schedules, loss weights, input resolution, detailed data splits, voxel-grid construction and fusion rules, and evaluation sampling are missing. Hardware and baseline timing comparisons are also absent.

The claim of scaling to hundreds of views exceeds the evidence: measurements stop at 64 views, and the paper acknowledges degradation beyond 32. Figure 6 also shows substantially superlinear runtime growth at larger view counts, contrary to the description of roughly linear scaling.

The separation of geometry prediction from style-conditioned appearance is sensible, and the qualitative results show appealing transfers across diverse scenes and artistic references.

The paper includes architectural and loss ablations, extensive qualitative examples, and inference-time and memory measurements.
weaknesses: The central attention distinction is mathematically unclear. With standard cross-attention and shared style keys/values, concatenating content queries across views gives exactly the concatenation of independently computed per-view outputs. Equations 1–2 therefore do not establish different coupling mechanisms or additional cross-view interaction. Any architectural differences responsible for Table 1 need to be specified.

The proposed 3D loss is inconsistently described. Equation 6 requires fused multi-view voxel features, but Algorithm 3 voxelizes each view separately and computes its statistics inside the view loop, without explicit cross-view fusion. Moreover, matching global moments does not itself guarantee correspondence-level consistency; the enforcement claims are too strong.

The evaluation protocol leaves important ambiguities. The paper does not specify correspondence warping, occlusion masking, evaluation-view selection, or clearly distinguish input-view reconstruction from held-out novel-view evaluation. Without these details, LPIPS/RMSE between views cannot reliably isolate stylization consistency from viewpoint changes or smoothing.

ArtScore measures reference-free artness, not fidelity to the requested style or preservation of content. No user study or complementary reference-conditioned assessment establishes the claimed best trade-off. Quantitative baseline comparisons cover only four scenes, without uncertainty estimates or clearly reported evaluation sample counts.

Novelty beyond combining VGGT/AnySplat with established style conditioning remains insufficiently isolated. The unavailable concurrent Styl3R implementation reasonably explains its omission, but comparisons against simpler feed-forward reconstruction-plus-stylization alternatives would still help establish the contribution.

Reproducibility is limited by missing training schedules, optimizer settings, loss weights, input resolutions, detailed voxel-fusion rules, and hardware specifications. The promised code release does not resolve the current methodological ambiguities.

The claim of scaling to hundreds of views exceeds the demonstrated evidence: efficiency measurements stop at 64 views, rendering cost is excluded, and the paper acknowledges declining visual quality above 32 views. Overall, the promising visual results do not outweigh the unresolved technical and evaluation issues.

strengths: The task is practically relevant: feed-forward stylization from unposed images removes per-scene optimization and external camera estimation, with potential benefits for interactive 3D content creation.
Separating geometry prediction from style-conditioned color prediction is a sensible design. Global content attention provides a plausible mechanism for coordinating appearance across views.

Table 3 reports consistently better short- and long-range consistency scores across all four evaluated scenes. Evaluation includes 50 unseen styles, held-out CO3D categories, and transfer from DL3DV to Tanks & Temples.

Qualitative examples demonstrate varied stylization and useful interpolation controls. The appendix provides training settings, additional examples, efficiency measurements, and explicit failure cases.
weaknesses: The methodological advance over VGGT/AnySplat, established style cross-attention, and the closely related feed-forward Styl3R is insufficiently isolated. There is no controlled comparison establishing how much improvement comes from the proposed stylization components versus the reconstruction backbone, training data, or input resolution.

Evidence for the central voxel-loss contribution is weak. In Table 2, scene-level versus voxel-level matching changes long-range LPIPS from 0.156 to 0.153 and ArtScore from 9.12 to 9.15, while short-range LPIPS is unchanged. These results cover only 15 scenes and lack uncertainty estimates. Moreover, matching statistics after voxel averaging does not directly penalize disagreement between corresponding views; inconsistent features can average out. The claim that this loss enforces cross-view consistency is stronger than the evidence.

The evaluation protocol leaves consequential details unclear: input-view counts for each method, separation of context and held-out target views, and the correspondence, warping, and visibility procedures used for consistency metrics. Appendix A.4 does not resolve these despite being cited for experimental details. This limits confidence in both novel-view generalization and comparative consistency claims.

The headline efficiency comparison is ambiguous. Table 4 reports 0.05 seconds for Stylos, whereas Appendix A.2 reports approximately 0.3 seconds for 1–2 views, 0.75 seconds for 16 views, and 4.83 seconds for 64 views, excluding rendering. Whether 0.05 seconds is amortized per view is unexplained. Comparisons also use different resolutions and combine scene fitting with rendering for optimization-based methods, without separately reporting reconstruction, style changes, and rendering costs.

The attention ablation evaluates reconstruction after Stage 1, not artistic stylization or cross-view consistency after Stage 2. Ablations of CLIP supervision, TV regularization, and relevant voxel-fusion choices are missing, leaving the sources of the reported improvements uncertain.

Broad scalability and quality claims exceed the demonstrated evidence. Efficiency measurements stop at 64 views, and quality reportedly degrades beyond 32, despite claims of scaling to hundreds. Stylos also trails G-Style on ArtFID in every main evaluation scene, and several supplementary content-preservation metrics are weaker; these trade-offs deserve substantive discussion.

Reproduction remains difficult despite the supplied hyperparameters: reconstruction, distillation, content, and CLIP losses are not fully specified, and important feature-fusion and evaluation details remain missing. Overall, the promising system results do not yet sufficiently establish the distinct contribution and reliability required for acceptance.

strengths: The task is practically relevant: producing stylized 3D Gaussians from unposed images without per-scene optimization could substantially simplify 3D content creation.

Separating geometry prediction from style-conditioned color prediction is a sensible design. Freezing geometry during stylization provides a clear mechanism for preserving the reconstructed structure.

The reported results are promising: Stylos leads all consistency metrics in Table 3 and achieves competitive artistic-quality scores across four scenes and 50 held-out styles. The qualitative examples demonstrate varied appearances and useful style interpolation.
The paper includes architectural and loss ablations, cross-category and cross-dataset evaluation, implementation details, and explicit visual failure cases.
weaknesses: The incremental contribution over existing components is insufficiently established. Geometry reconstruction and Gaussian construction largely follow VGGT and AnySplat, cross-attention style conditioning follows established practice, and Styl3R already addresses feedforward stylized reconstruction. The experiments do not adequately isolate which proposed additions explain the advantage over this closest baseline.

Evidence for the central voxel-loss contribution is weak. In Table 2, moving from scene-level to voxel-level loss changes ArtScore only from 9.12 to 9.15, leaves short-range LPIPS unchanged at 0.047, and improves long-range LPIPS from 0.156 to 0.153. Without uncertainty estimates or broader ablations, these small differences do not establish a meaningful advantage. Matching global statistics after voxel fusion also does not directly penalize disagreement between observations fused into the same voxel, so claims that it enforces cross-view consistency are overstated.

The evaluation protocol leaves important comparability questions unresolved. Appendix A.4 uses full-resolution inputs for optimization-based methods, 256×256 for Styl3R, and 448×448 for Stylos, without clearly specifying a common evaluation resolution. Input-view budgets, held-out target-view selection, and the warping, visibility masking, and camera alignment used for consistency metrics are insufficiently described. These details materially affect the headline comparisons.

The efficiency claim is not adequately supported by consistent timing definitions. Table 4 reports 0.05 seconds, whereas Appendix A.2 reports approximately 0.3 seconds for one view, 0.75 seconds for 16 views, and 4.83 seconds for 64 views, excluding rendering. Whether Table 4 measures amortized per-view time or another quantity is unexplained. Reconstruction, style application, and rendering costs should be separated to substantiate the real-time claim.

The ablations do not establish several central claims. The attention comparison measures reconstruction after Stage 1 rather than artistic fidelity and consistency after stylization; CLIP, reconstruction, and TV losses are not isolated. Quantitative comparison is limited to four scenes, and scaling to hundreds of views is not demonstrated: measurements stop at 64 views, with acknowledged quality degradation above 32.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix. Reconstruction, distillation, and CLIP objectives are not fully specified, and several feature-loss and evaluation details are missing. The supplied manuscript contains blank resource links and inconsistent statements about code availability. These gaps, together with the unresolved evaluation issues, prevent a confident acceptance recommendation.

strengths: The problem is practically relevant: feed-forward stylization from unposed images avoids scene-specific optimization and combines reconstruction and artistic appearance transfer in one pipeline.

Separating frozen geometry prediction from style-conditioned Gaussian colors is sensible and supports controllable stylization. The qualitative examples demonstrate varied styles and smooth style interpolation.

Table 3 reports consistently better short- and long-range consistency across all four evaluated scenes. Testing on held-out CO3D categories, different scene datasets, and 50 unseen styles provides useful evidence of generalization.
The appendix includes implementation settings, additional comparisons, scaling measurements, and candid failure cases.
weaknesses: The incremental contribution over VGGT/AnySplat reconstruction, established cross-attention conditioning, and the closely related Styl3R is insufficiently isolated. The attention ablation measures reconstruction after Stage 1 rather than actual stylization quality or consistency, so it does not establish the claimed benefit of global conditioning for the target task.

Evidence for the central voxel-space loss is weak relative to the simpler scene-level loss. In Table 2, ArtScore improves only from 9.12 to 9.15, short-range LPIPS is unchanged, and long-range LPIPS improves from 0.156 to 0.153, without uncertainty estimates. Matching global statistics after voxel fusion does not directly penalize disagreement between views; inconsistent features can average to the same voxel features. The stronger claim that this objective enforces cross-view coherence needs better justification and controlled experiments.

The headline timing is unresolved. Table 4 reports 0.05 seconds for Stylos, whereas Appendix A.2 reports approximately 0.3 seconds for one or two views, 0.75 seconds for 16 views, and 4.83 seconds for 64 views, excluding rendering. A per-view amortized number and complete scene latency must be distinguished before claiming the fastest stylization or practical real-time reconstruction.

The comparison protocol leaves material confounds. Appendix A.4 uses full-resolution images for optimization methods, 256×256 for Styl3R, and 448×448 for Stylos, without clearly specifying a common metric resolution. Input-view budgets, held-out rendering splits, and the correspondence, warping, and visibility procedures for consistency metrics are insufficiently described. These omissions make the reported advantages difficult to assess or reproduce.

Artistic-quality evidence is mixed: G-Style has better ArtFID on all four scenes, while supplementary content-preservation metrics frequently favor other methods. No perceptual study resolves these trade-offs. Quantitative scene coverage is limited, and claims of scalability to hundreds of views exceed the demonstrated measurements, which stop at 64 views and already show quality degradation.

Important training details remain underspecified, including the exact reconstruction and CLIP objectives during stylization and aspects of feature unprojection and masking. Overall, the promising system and reported results do not yet overcome the unresolved contribution, evaluation, and efficiency issues required for acceptance at a selective conference.
